author: Goodenough, W. H.
title: Native Astronomy in the Central Carolines
venue: Museum Monographs, University Museum, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia
claim: The central Carolinian sidereal compass: Altair (mailap) is the base star, its rising marking east and its setting west; Polaris marks north and the upright Southern Cross south; twenty-eight further points are marked by the rising and setting of other stars, 32 in all; the rising points run from Polaris through beta Ursae Minoris (Kochab), alpha Ursae Majoris (Dubhe), alpha Cassiopeiae, Vega, the Pleiades, Aldebaran, gamma Aquilae, Altair, beta Aquilae and Orion's Belt, and on through Antares to the Southern Cross, which occupies five compass positions; where the stars physically rise the points are not equally spaced; in a summary of his account, the stars name the points rather than physically marking them.
verified: Structure (Altair base star, 'rising marks due east ... setting due west', Polaris just visible and north, Southern Cross upright south, 'twenty-eight additional points', not equally spaced) confirmed from WebSearch extracts of the Penn Museum PDF. Revision: further extracts of the same PDF list the rising points in order, including the Pleiades, Alpha Tauri (Aldebaran), Gamma Aquilae, Alpha Aquilae (Altair), Beta Aquilae and Orion's Belt, and its list of plates includes 'The Southern Cross at Compass Positions 15-19'; so every point on the page's ring is in Goodenough's compass, and the earlier 'one source' (hollow) marking of the Pleiades, Aldebaran, Tarazed, Alshain, Orion's Belt and the leaning Cross was wrong. Two search summaries (one of an eHRAF reprint) say he argued that the stars name the points rather than physically mark them; the page reports that as a summary. An eHRAF summary notes that nearly all of his data were compiled from published sources. I still could not read the monograph's table or plates themselves; the PDF host was not reachable from the sandbox.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Goodenough 1953 Native Astronomy in the Central Carolines star compass'; 'Carolinian star compass 32 points Altair Mailap Goodenough'; revision: 'Native Astronomy in the Central Carolines "Alpha Tauri" "Pleiades" "Gamma Aquilae" "Beta Aquilae" "Orion"'; 'Native Astronomy in the Central Carolines Southern Cross rising upright setting positions compass points'; 'Goodenough sidereal compass star structure stars do not physically mark the points they name them'

author: Gladwin, T.
title: East Is a Big Bird: Navigation and Logic on Puluwat Atoll
claim: Etak as Gladwin learned it on Puluwat from the navigator Hipour in the 1960s: a reference island off to one side of the course moves backward under successive star points; etak as a way of organising known information about speed, time, geography and stars into an estimate of distance, not a belief that islands move. Also the source of the 'big bird' gloss of Altair that Holton et al. 2015 dispute.
verified: Publisher, year and the Hipour apprenticeship confirmed from the Harvard University Press listing and catalogue records. The description of etak and of Gladwin's view of it is confirmed only through secondary accounts (Hutchins's work, Riesenberg 1975's summary, Futility Closet's quotation via Magnani 2001); I could not read the book. The page paraphrases rather than quotes it.

claim: The Puluwat–Truk (Chuuk) voyage with Pisaras as the reference island; navigators' term rendered as 'dragging'; Pisaras dragged through the risings of Vega, Cassiopeia, the main star of Ursa Major, Kochab and Polaris, ending at Vega's setting on arrival; the course from Puluwat to Truk almost directly east on the rising of Altair.
verified: From WebSearch extracts of the Penn Museum's online reprint, across three searches. The title appears both as 'A Search for Pattern' and 'A Search for a Pattern' in catalogue records. I did not see the article's figure, so the eight-segment count on the page is my geometry, consistent with (not copied from) the record; one search summary also reported 'eight segments' for this example. Revision: the page no longer presents the match of the in-between star sequence as an independent confirmation. Given the two end bearings (Pisaras under rising Vega from Puluwat and setting Vega from Chuuk), the order of the seven points in between is forced by the compass; the geometry tests only the two ends.

The page uses it for local names and spellings, the east-up layout, the leaning-Cross definition and the star positions; after the revision it is no longer the only evidence for any compass point. The first version wrongly called the 45° definition the author's own and gave all three Southern Cross positions the star name Ubw.
